title: Token-tiling and quant-scheduler proposal for mixed-interaction workloads (draft)
body:
Purpose and scope:

This note sketches a complementary set of recommendations — token-tiling, slice-aware batching, and a lightweight quant-scheduler — aimed at reducing unit token costs for mixed-interaction workloads (short prompts, long completions, and multi-turn chat) while preserving latency SLOs. The goal is to provide an actionable tuning checklist + a small spreadsheet schema (see linked artifacts) so SRE/product teams can run quick cost vs latency sweeps.

Motivation (what problem we see):
- Many customers have heterogenous request mixes: frequent short completions (<= 32 tokens) plus occasional long generative sessions (>512 tokens). Current global batching and qcache defaults either favor throughput (large batch) and inflate latency on short requests, or favor latency (tiny batch) and waste GPU cycles on long sessions.
- Quantization profiles today are coarse: a single qconfig per model or per-route. That misses opportunity to use slightly lower-precision paths for cache/warm requests and keep higher precision for cold or fidelity-sensitive calls.
- Cache TTLs are uniform, leading to over-eviction for stable sessions and under-utilization for repetitive short prompts.

Key ideas (high-level):
1) Token-tiling: dynamically group requests by predicted token-lifecycle (short, medium, long) into separate tiling lanes. Each lane has tuned batching size and max-latency target.
2) Slice-aware batching: within a GPU worker group, reserve micro-slices (time windows) for short-lane micro-batches to meet tail latency; accumulate long-lane batches over slightly longer windows for throughput.
3) Quant-scheduler: schedule quantization level by request cohort + cache/warmth signal. Use stochastic lower-bit fallback for highly cacheable/low-variance completions, and conservative (higher bit) paths for cold starts or eval routes.
4) TTL-cohorts for qcache: per-cohort TTLs (e.g., 1m for ephemeral chat, 30m for repeated search-like prompts) to balance hit rate and memory.

Operational knobs to expose (recommended defaults in spreadsheet):
- lane_cutoffs: ["short<=32","medium<=256","long>256"] (editable)
- short_lane_batch_target_tokens: 512 (i.e., batch up to ~16 short requests if avg short=32)
- short_lane_max_latency_ms: 60ms (SLO-sensitive)
- medium_lane_batch_target_tokens: 4096
- medium_lane_max_latency_ms: 120ms
- long_lane_batch_target_tokens: 16384
- quant_schedule: {"warm_hit": "int8-fast", "cold": "int16-accurate", "high_quality_route": "fp16"} (see spreadsheet column examples)
- qcache_ttl_by_cohort: ["short:60","medium:900","long:3600"] (seconds)

Notes on latency accounting and configuration:
- Target token-based batching (batch_target_tokens) is a more stable control than requests-per-batch when request lengths vary drastically. The runtime should convert batch_target_tokens to request batch counts per lane based on recent moving-average request length.
- short_lane_max_latency_ms must be enforced at dispatcher level via micro-slice preemption: if an in-flight long-batch has not completed and a short request arrives, urgent short-lane micro-batch is flushed early (even if below target tokens) to meet tail latency. This reduces theoretical throughput but preserves UX.

Quant-scheduler operational model (practical):
- Signal inputs: (a) cache_hit (binary), (b) request_route_quality_flag (e.g., eval or production), (c) recent_cohort_variance (stddev of top-p results or embedding similarity), (d) explicit quality override from client.
- Decision rules (simple to start):
  - If cache_hit && cohort_variance < threshold -> use int8-fast path with KV cache enabled.
  - Else if route == high_quality -> use fp16 or int16-accurate path.
  - Else if resource_pressure (GPU util > 85%) -> fall back to int8 with token-budget weighting (lower priority).
- Implementation note: prefer having both int8 and int16 kernels available in each worker; switching is a dispatch-time table selection rather than model reloading. For older infra lacking int8 kernels, schedule int16 as the fallback.

Cache TTL cohorts and eviction heuristics: simple heuristics reduce ops complexity while achieving most benefit:
- Cohorts defined by prompt hash prefix + route tag + user_cohort_id(optional).
- Eviction: LRU per-cohort with soft TTL; when memory pressure spikes, reduce per-cohort TTL multiplicatively (e.g., /2) rather than evicting randomly.
- Proactive warming: when a request is sampled as high-probability repeat (observed repeat rate > 2%), create a transient prefetch into qcache on slot idle cycles.

Spreadsheet schema (what you can run quickly):
- Input columns: avg_request_length_by_route, pct_short_requests, avg_turns_per_session, baseline_latency_ms, baseline_cost_per_token, current_qconfig
- Sweep columns: short_lane_max_latency_ms, batch_target_tokens_short, batch_target_tokens_medium, batch_target_tokens_long, qcache_ttl_short, qcache_ttl_medium, qcache_ttl_long, expected_qcache_hit_rate
- Outputs (computed): projected_throughput_rps, projected_avg_latency_ms, projected_tail_p95_latency_ms, projected_cost_per_token_effective, estimated_monthly_cost_delta
- I included a sample tab in the linked spreadsheet that runs a 3x3 sweep for short_lane_max_latency_ms x batch_target_tokens_short and computes cost/latency tradeoffs.

Safety and quality guardrails:
- Canary rollout: always roll quant-scheduler changes behind a canary cohort with per-prompt quality checks (BLEU/ROUGE proxies or a small set of golden prompts).
- Regression detection: set automated alerts for quality drift on 50 golden prompts (alerts trigger if avg similarity drops > 2%).
- Fallback policy: if quality alert fires, route affected traffic to the higher-precision variant and incrementally revert recent q-scheduler rules.

SRE/infra considerations (implementation rough order-of-effort):
- Low effort: dispatcher lanes + micro-slice flush; TTL-cohort bookkeeping in qcache; spreadsheet and runbook for tuning.
- Medium effort: kernel availability and hot-switch cost accounting; metrics and tracing for per-lane latencies and per-qconfig quality signals.
- Higher effort: predictive prefetching (based on session models) and dynamic cohort resizing with ML-driven thresholds.

Practical recomenda tions (quick checklist for an experiment):
1) Pick a candidate tenant with 50–200k daily tokens and mixed traffic (search + chat).
2) Baseline: collect 72 hours of per-route length distribution and current qcache hit rates.
3) Configure lanes with cutoffs [<=32, 33-256, >256] and set short_lane_max_latency_ms=60, batch_target_tokens_short=512.
4) Enable int8-fast for cache_hit-only cohort and keep fp16 for cold routes.
5) Run 48-hour canary, monitor cost delta, avg latency, p95 tail, and golden-prompt similarity.
6) If p95 < baseline_p95 + 10% and golden prompt similarity delta < 2%, promote to wider cohort and run 7-day sweep on batch sizes.

Open questions / unresolved items:
- What exact thresholds for cohort_variance are signalively useful across customers? We need to instrument a couple of tenants to collect distribution stats.
- How often do we want to recompute the lane cutoffs? Per-hour? Per-day?
- Is the additional complexity of maintaining multiple kernels per worker justified vs. model-variant approach (separate lightweight model replicas per quant level)?

Next steps (short runway):
- Lina to produce a small sample dataset extractor (2 days) for per-route length distributions.
- Marco to add a short tab in the existing optimize spreadsheet with the sweep template (1 day).
- Ravi to prototype dispatcher micro-slice flush in the staging runtime (3 weeks).
- I'll own the canary run and quality monitoring setup (2 weeks).

If useful I can convert this into a short playbook with exact REST flags to flip for canary and a sample CLI to run the spreadsheet sweep. Comments welcome — this is intentionally pragmatic and tuned to get measurable unit-cost wins while keeping rollback simple.

---
Notes: inspired by several internal presets but tries to be orthogonal to the existing qcache/batch playbooks by focusing on lane-based tiling and a light-weight quant scheduling layer that trades precision only where safe.
